# Conclusion

This study asked whether a human's emotional state, as measured through
FER and HRV, can be predicted above chance from a plant's
electrophysiological signal alone. A multimodal pilot study with 15
participants was conducted, combining heart rate variability and facial
expression recognition into proxy indicators of arousal and valence, with
ambient CO~2~ recorded alongside. The plant signal was evaluated against
these indicators since no self-reported ground truth was collected.

The answer to the study's main question is a qualified yes. Valence
classification produced the clearest result (macro-F1 = 0.42,
permutation p = 0.005) and recognized all three classes with comparable
reliability, but at 43% accuracy against the approximately 33% expected
by chance it is a statistical association across 284 windows and 15
participants, not a channel from which the state of an individual could
be read at a practically useful rate. The five-class emotion label
likewise reached significance (p = 0.015), yet its macro-F1 of 0.21 lies
close to the uniform-chance expectation of approximately 0.20, and its
42% accuracy rests on the dominant neutral class; a label crossing
valence with arousal cannot carry more than its weaker component, and
arousal, resting solely on HRV, did not reach conventional significance
(p = 0.055). H1 is therefore supported for valence, only nominally for
the crossed emotion label, and not for arousal. The difference between
the two dimensions should not be read as evidence about the dimensions
themselves, since they were operationalized through proxies of unequal
quality, a facial expression model on the one hand and a single HRV
index on the other.

The secondary analysis tested a plausible alternative explanation
for the valence finding, that ambient CO~2~ rather than the plant tracked
the participant's breathing and thus their emotional state. It does not
hold: the plant--valence association survives controlling for CO~2~
almost unchanged at both the raw and the session-normalized level. 
The plant therefore does not follow the air on the timescale at which the 
classification operates.
The data provides no support for H2, which given the sample size should be
read as absence of evidence rather than as definitive proof.

These findings must be read against several structural limitations. All
results are validated only against proxy labels; the sample is small,
single-cohort, and recorded on a single day; the fixed stimulus order
leaves session time as an unresolved confound; and no sham or shielding
control rules out electromagnetic artifacts. The mechanism also remains
open: excluding CO~2~ removes an obvious mediating pathway without
putting another in its place. Future work should prioritize a larger
cohort with validated self-report ratings and arousal markers beyond
RMSSD, and should replicate the present design across a broader
population to determine whether the weak but statistically robust
valence signal reflects a reproducible phenomenon.
